title: Al-Masad: the palm-fiber rope
hookLine: a warning about Abu Lahab, the Prophet's own uncle and enemy (Surah 111)

cards: Every family has someone. The uncle who turns every holiday dinner into an argument. The cousin who takes your news and makes it about himself.
Most of the time it's small. For the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ it was not small. His uncle, his father's own brother, became one of his fiercest public enemies.
And the Qur'an names him, by his nickname, in a surah of its own.

teach.h: A CALL FROM THE HILL OF SAFA.
teach.b: The story is in Sahih al-Bukhari. Told to warn his own clan, the Prophet climbed the hill of Safa in Mecca and called out to the families of Quraysh, one by one, until they gathered.
He asked: if I told you an army was behind this hill, would you believe me? We've never known you to lie, they said. Then, he said, I am a warner to you before a severe punishment.
His uncle, Abu Lahab, answered: may you perish! Is this what you gathered us for? The surah answers him with his own word.

teach.h: MAY YOU PERISH — HIS UNCLE'S ANSWER.
teach.b: Pickthall translates the first line: The power of Abu Lahab will perish, and he will perish. Abu Lahab wasn't his real name. It means father of flame, a nickname, some say for his glowing, ruddy face.
The surah says his wealth and his gains won't help him. It mentions his wife too, though not by name; commentators say she scattered thorns in the Prophet's path.
She'll carry firewood, with a rope of palm fiber, masad, around her neck. The surah is named for that rope. Here's what scholars point out.
Being the Prophet's uncle, the closest possible tie, didn't protect Abu Lahab. And the reverse is in the same story: another uncle, Abu Talib, protected the Prophet for years.
Two brothers, the same nephew, two different choices.
Kin is not a guarantee, not of harm, not of goodness. What counts, in the Qur'an's telling, is what each person does.

how: Surah al-Masad, also called al-Lahab, is recited in the prayers like other short surahs; Muslims learn its story, the Prophet's call from Safa and his uncle's reply, as part of the life of the Prophet.

o: a bundle of firewood for burning
a rope of twisted palm fiber
a flame, as in the name Abu Lahab

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.
p: father of flame, the uncle who opposed
the hill where he called his clan

s: Abu Lahab was the Prophet's real uncle
his father's brother, and one of his fiercest public enemies.
Abu Lahab was his birth name
it's a nickname: father of flame. some say for his glowing face.
the surah names Abu Lahab's wife
it calls her the carrier of firewood; her name comes from the commentators.

games.q: the Prophet calls his clan to the hill of Safa and warns them. his uncle speaks first. what does he say?
o: may you perish! is this why you gathered us?
games.why: Abu Lahab cursed him, and the surah answers with his own word: the power of Abu Lahab will perish (Bukhari).

practice: Think of your family, the one you were born into or the one you've made: one person whose closeness has been a gift, and one relationship where being related hasn't made things good. Hold both as true, without judging either.
Then turn it around, gently: being part of a family isn't a guarantee for you either, so what would you want your own choices to add?

wordCard.voice: Al-Masad. The palm-fiber rope, the name of Surah one hundred eleven, about the Prophet's uncle Abu Lahab. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: twisted fiber, a rope of palm fiber; the last word of Surah 111.

carryVoice: Your line: kin is not a guarantee. Two uncles, one nephew, two different choices. That's day one hundred sixty-three.
